Dhritarashtra.description: The blind old king of the Kauravas, father of Duryodhana, who asks Sanjaya to narrate the events of the Kurukshetra war.

Sanjaya.description: Dhritarashtra's minister and charioteer, granted divine vision by Vyasa to narrate the events of the battlefield.

Arjuna.description: Arjuna is a principal Pandava prince and the main hero of the Bhagavad Geeta, addressed by many epithets denoting his lineage, valor, and relationship to his mother Kunti.

Krishna.description: The Supreme Being and charioteer of Arjuna, also known by his clan name Vrishni and as the slayer of the demon Keshi.

Duryodhana.description: The eldest son of Dhritarashtra and leader of the Kauravas, depicted as a tyrant and the main antagonist.

Drona.description: The teacher of both Pandavas and Kauravas and a key commander in the Kaurava army.

Bhishma.description: Bhishma is the grandsire of both Pandavas and Kauravas, a revered elder and commander of the Kaurava forces in the Mahabharata.

Bhima.description: One of the Pandava brothers, known for his immense strength and valor.

Virata.description: A king allied with the Pandavas, commander in their army.

Drupada.description: King of Panchala, father of Draupadi and Dhristadyumna, and an ally of the Pandavas.

Dhrishtaketu.description: A warrior allied with the Pandavas.

Chekitana.description: A notable warrior in the Pandava army.

Kashi.description: Refers to the king of Kashi, an archer allied with the Pandavas.

Purujit.description: A commander in the Pandava army.

Kuntibhoja.description: A king allied with the Pandavas.

Saibya.description: A warrior allied with the Pandavas.

Yudhamanyu.description: A strong warrior in the Pandava army.

Uttamaujas.description: A brave commander in the Pandava army.

Draupadi.description: Wife of the Pandavas, whose sons fight in the war.

Karna.description: A great warrior and ally of the Kauravas.

Kripa.description: A teacher and warrior fighting for the Kauravas.

Aswatthama.description: Son of Drona, a formidable warrior on the Kaurava side.

Vikarna.description: A Kaurava prince and brother of Duryodhana.

Somadatta.description: Father of Bhurishrava, a warrior in the Kaurava army.

Yudhisthira.description: Eldest of the Pandava brothers, known for his righteousness.

Nakula.description: One of the Pandava twins, renowned for his skills.

Sahadeva.description: The other Pandava twin, skilled in warfare.

Shikhandi.description: A commander in the Pandava army, instrumental in Bhishma's fall.

Satyaki.description: A hero, charioteer, and commander in the Pandava army, also known as Yuyudhana.

Hanuman.description: The monkey-god, whose symbol is Arjuna's chariot ensign.

Pandu.description: Father of the Pandavas, the five brothers who are central to the Mahabharata.

Pandavas.description: The Pandavas are the five sons of Pandu, protagonists in the Mahabharata.

Kurukshetra.description: The holy battlefield where the Mahabharata war takes place.

Vyasa.description: Vyasa, also known as Veda Vyasa, is the sage who composed the Mahabharata and the Bhagavad Gita and compiled the Vedas.

Hastinapura.description: The capital city of the Kauravas and Pandavas.

Kauravas.description: The sons of Dhritarashtra, antagonists in the Mahabharata.

Aryan.description: Refers to the ancient Indo-Aryan culture and people.

Mahabharata.description: The great Indian epic that contains the Bhagavad Geeta.

Bhagawad Geeta.description: The Bhagavad Geeta is a sacred Hindu scripture, part of the Mahabharata, consisting of a dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna on spiritual and ethical matters.

Hindu.description: Pertaining to the religious, cultural, and philosophical traditions of India.

Brahmana.description: Brahmana (or Brahmin) refers to a member of the priestly class in the traditional Hindu caste system, known as the 'twice-born' due to their spiritual initiation.

Shastra.description: Shastra refers to scriptural texts or treatises in Hindu tradition, providing authoritative teachings and guidance.

Artha Shastra.description: An ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, politics, and economics.

Vrishni-clan.description: The lineage or clan to which Krishna belongs.

Upanishads.description: The Upanishads are ancient Hindu philosophical texts exploring spiritual knowledge and the nature of reality.

Brahman.description: Brahman is the ultimate, all-pervading, unchanging reality or God-principle in Vedanta philosophy.

Brahma-Vidya.description: Knowledge of Brahman, the Supreme Reality.

Yoga Shastra.description: The science or scripture of Yoga, outlining its philosophy and practice.

Sankalpa Vakya.description: A traditional epilogue or concluding statement marking the end of a chapter in Hindu scriptures.

Aryan-culture.description: The cultural and spiritual heritage of the ancient Aryans.

Yoga.description: A spiritual discipline or path aiming at union with the Divine or Self-realization.

maharathas.description: Great warriors capable of fighting multiple opponents, often commanding large divisions.

acharya.description: A respected teacher or preceptor, especially in spiritual or scriptural matters.

Atatayinah.description: Felons or aggressors deserving punishment according to ancient law.

Dharma.description: Righteousness, duty, or the moral law governing individual conduct.

Kula-Dharma.description: The specific duties and traditions of a family.

Kshatriyas.description: The warrior and ruling class in the traditional Hindu social order.

Vaishyas.description: The merchant and agricultural class in the traditional Hindu social order.

Shudras.description: The laborer and service class in the traditional Hindu social order.

Moksha.description: Spiritual liberation or Self-realization, the ultimate goal in Hindu philosophy.

Kshema.description: Material and physical well-being or security.

Sadhana.description: Spiritual practice or discipline undertaken to achieve a goal.

Mantra.description: A sacred utterance, sound, or phrase used in spiritual practice.

Sankalpa.description: A resolve or intention, often recited as a formal statement in rituals.

Kunti.description: The mother of Arjuna and the Pandavas, also known as Pritha.

Muni.description: A term for a sage or silent wise man, used to describe the realized person.

Hindus.description: Followers of Hinduism, the religious tradition to which the Gita belongs.

Hinduism.description: The major Indian religious tradition, whose philosophy and practices are discussed in the Gita.

Sanatana Dharma.description: A term meaning 'eternal law', referring to the eternal and universal principles of Hinduism.

Veera-Swarga.description: The 'Heaven of the Heroes', a celestial realm attained by those who die heroically in battle.

Vedanta.description: Vedanta is a major school of Hindu philosophy based on the teachings of the Upanishads, with followers known as Vedantins.

Karma Kanda.description: The ritualistic portion of the Vedas, focused on prescribed actions and rituals.

Samadhi.description: A state of deep meditative absorption or superconsciousness.

Sankhya.description: Sankhya is a classical Indian philosophical system explaining reality through dual principles of Purusha (spirit) and Prakriti (matter), with followers known as Sankhyans.

Karma Yoga.description: Karma Yoga is the path of selfless action, performing one's duties without attachment to results as a means to spiritual realization.

Brahmi-sthitih.description: The state of being established in Brahman, or Self-realization.

Adharma.description: Unrighteousness; actions or qualities contrary to Dharma.

Swadharma.description: One's own duty or personal call-of-character, according to one's nature and position.

Manava Dharma.description: The essential duty or law of human beings, emphasizing their divine nature.

Atman.description: Atman is the individual Self or soul, the innermost essence of a being, also referred to as the Self in Vedanta philosophy.

Vasanas.description: Vasanas are mental impressions or tendencies formed by past actions and desires, driving future behavior.

Viveka.description: Discrimination or discernment, especially between the real and the unreal.

Indriyas.description: The sense-organs or faculties of perception and action.

Karma.description: Karma refers to action or deed and its resulting effects, embodying the law of cause and effect governing all actions.

Karma-phala.description: The fruits or results of actions.

Buddhi yoga.description: The yoga of wisdom or devotion through the intellect; acting with a steady, discriminative mind.

Gunas.description: The gunas are the three fundamental qualities—Sattwa (purity), Rajas (activity), and Tamas (inertia)—that constitute nature and influence all beings.

Sattwa.description: The quality of purity, harmony, and balance.

Rajas.description: The quality of activity, passion, and restlessness.

Tamas.description: The quality of inertia, darkness, and ignorance.

Dwandwas.description: Pairs of opposites, such as pleasure and pain, success and failure.

Pratyahara.description: Withdrawal of the senses from their objects, a yogic practice.

Pranayama.description: Control of the breath, a yogic discipline.

Uparati.description: Withdrawal or cessation from worldly activities; inner quietude.

Maya.description: The cosmic illusion that veils the true nature of reality.

Avarana-Shakti.description: The veiling power of Maya, which obscures the Self.

Vikshepa-Shakti.description: The projecting power of Maya, which creates the appearance of the world.

Prasada.description: Prasada refers to mental peace, tranquility, or clarity resulting from self-control and purity of mind.

Nishkama.description: Without desire; acting without selfish motives.

Shrutam.description: That which has been heard; scriptural or traditional knowledge.

Shrotavyam.description: That which is yet to be heard; future knowledge or experiences.

Sthita-Prajna.description: One of steady wisdom; a person established in Self-knowledge.

Samnyasin.description: A renunciate; one who has given up worldly attachments and desires.

Janaka.description: A wise king cited as an example of one who attained perfection through action (Karma Yoga).

Ashwapati.description: Another ancient king mentioned as an exemplar of attaining perfection through right action.

Prajapati.description: The Creator deity in Hindu cosmology, said to have created mankind and sacrifice together.

Vrindavana.description: A town associated with Krishna's early life and divine play.

gopis.description: The cowherd maidens of Vrindavana, devotees of Krishna.

Kamadhuk.description: The mythological wish-fulfilling cow, also called Kamadhenu, symbolizing abundance.

Kamadhenu.description: A mythological cow said to grant all desires, referenced as a symbol of infinite potential.

Devas.description: The gods or divine forces in Hindu cosmology, representing various aspects of the universal power.

Mother India.description: A personification of India as a nurturing mother, symbolizing the nation's productive potential.

Shankara.description: Adi Shankaracharya, a renowned Vedantic philosopher and commentator.

Bharatas.description: A term referring to the descendants of King Bharata, often used for Arjuna and his kin.

Varna.description: The term for caste or class in Hindu society, based on individual temperament and duties.

Loka-sangraha.description: A Sanskrit term meaning 'welfare of the world', used to describe selfless action for the greater good.

Tattwavit.description: A knower of the Reality or Truth, an epithet for the wise or enlightened person.

Buddha.description: Here, refers to an enlightened being or sage, not specifically Gautama Buddha.

YOGA.description: A spiritual discipline or path, especially as systematized in the Gita.

Jnana Yoga.description: Jnana Yoga is the path of knowledge, focusing on the realization of the Self through wisdom, discrimination, and contemplation.

Prakriti.description: Nature or the fundamental creative energy, consisting of the three gunas.

Niyatam Karma.description: Obligatory or prescribed duty, actions one is bound to perform.

Yajna.description: Yajna is sacrifice or ritual offering, often symbolizing selfless action and dedication in spiritual practice.

Seva.description: Seva is selfless service, often performed as an act of devotion or for the welfare of others.

Annam.description: Food; that which nourishes living beings.

Shraddha.description: Shraddha is faith or conviction, considered the guiding force behind actions and spiritual progress.

Anasuyantah.description: Without cavilling or fault-finding; accepting teachings without negative criticism.

Jnana.description: Knowledge, especially spiritual wisdom or discrimination.

Adhyatma Chetasa.description: Mind absorbed in the Self; spiritual consciousness.

Karya.description: Effect or result, especially of action.

Prarabdha.description: The portion of past karma that is responsible for the present birth and circumstances.

Mukta.description: A liberated soul, free from bondage.

Matam.description: Opinion or doctrine, especially in a religious or philosophical context.

Vivasvan.description: The Sun-god, to whom Krishna says he first imparted the ancient Yoga at the beginning of creation.

Manu.description: The ancient law-giver of India, son of Vivasvan, who received the knowledge of Yoga from his father.

Ikshvaku.description: The ancestor of the Solar-dynasty, who received the knowledge from Manu.

Ayodhya.description: An ancient city in India, historically ruled by the Solar-dynasty.

Pauranic.description: Relating to the Puranas, ancient Hindu texts that elaborate on mythology and philosophy.

Gokula.description: The village associated with Krishna's childhood.

Solar-dynasty.description: A royal lineage in ancient India, said to descend from the Sun-god.

Tapo-yajna.description: Sacrifice in the form of austerity or penance.

Yoga-yajna.description: Sacrifice in the form of spiritual discipline or Yoga.

Swadhyaya-yajna.description: Sacrifice in the form of scriptural study.

Brahma-Yajna.description: Sacrifice offered to Brahman, or the pursuit of spiritual knowledge.

Achirena.description: A Sanskrit term meaning 'ere long' or 'soon,' indicating the quick attainment of the goal.

Param Shantim.description: Sanskrit for 'Supreme Peace,' the ultimate goal described in the Gita.

Avatara.description: Divine incarnation; the descent of God into a physical form.

Kshatriya.description: The warrior or ruler class in the varna system.

Shudra.description: The servant or laborer class in the varna system.

Avidya.description: Avidya is ignorance, particularly of the true nature of the Self.

Saguna.description: With attributes or qualities; refers to worship of God with form.

Nirguna.description: Without attributes or qualities; refers to worship of the formless absolute.

Ajah.description: Unborn; a term for the eternal, birthless reality.

Kavi.description: A seer or poet, especially one with spiritual insight.

Prana.description: Prana is the vital energy or life-force that sustains the body and its functions.

Kumbhaka.description: The retention or holding of breath in pranayama.

Tatparah.description: Devoted to or intent on (the spiritual goal).

Samshaya-atma.description: The doubting self; one who is afflicted by doubt.

Atmavantah.description: One who is poised in the Self.

Advaita.description: A non-dualistic school of Vedanta philosophy that teaches the oneness of Atman and Brahman.

Patanjali Yoga-Sutra.description: A classical text on Yoga philosophy, outlining the eightfold path of Yoga.

Goutama-Smriti.description: An ancient Hindu legal and ethical text, quoted by Shankara in his commentary.

Maheshwara.description: A title meaning 'Great Lord,' often referring to the Supreme Being or Shiva.

Sarva-Loka-Maheshwarah.description: A Sanskrit epithet meaning 'Great Lord of all worlds,' used for the Supreme Self in the Gita.

Karma-Samnyasa-Yoga.description: The Yoga of renunciation of action, involving giving up the sense of doership.

Sakshibhava.description: The witness-attitude; observing one's actions and thoughts with detachment.

Swabhava.description: Swabhava is one's own nature or inherent disposition, determining character and actions.

Dwaitins.description: Followers of the Dvaita (dualistic) school of Vedanta philosophy.

Ishwara.description: The Lord or Supreme Controller, often referring to God as the ruler of the universe.

Paramatman.description: The Supreme Self, the universal consciousness underlying all beings.

Samattwam.description: Equanimity or mental evenness, a key quality in spiritual realization.

Sama-darshin.description: One who sees with equal vision; a sage who perceives the same Self in all beings.

Dhyana Yoga.description: The path of meditation, leading to steady contemplation and realization of the Self.

Rama Tirtha.description: A Hindu saint referenced for his teachings on the consequences of sin.

Ganges.description: A sacred river in India, often associated with spiritual purification and meditation.

Jamuna.description: A river in India, also known as Yamuna, associated with Krishna's pastimes.

Kusha.description: A type of sacred grass traditionally used in Vedic rituals and for meditation seats.

Asana.description: A physical posture or seat, especially for meditation.

Pariah.description: A term for an outcaste or someone of low social status in traditional Indian society.

Prasthana Traya.description: The collective term for the three foundational texts of Vedanta: the Upanishads, Brahmasutra, and Bhagavad Gita.

Yogi.description: A Yogi or Yogin is one who practices Yoga and seeks spiritual realization; Yogins are practitioners of Yoga.

Arurukshah.description: A seeker who desires to ascend the path of Yoga.

Yoga-Arudhah.description: One who has attained mastery in Yoga; established in meditation.

Shama.description: Quiescence or mental tranquillity; control of the mind.

Aparigraha.description: Non-possessiveness; freedom from hoarding or attachment to possessions.

Sthiram.description: Steady or firm, especially in posture.

Brahmacharya.description: Celibacy or self-control, especially in relation to sense impulses.

Nirvana.description: Liberation; the state of ultimate freedom from suffering.

Shantam.description: Peaceful; the state of absolute peace.

Swapna.description: Dream; also refers to the state of conscious experience.

Avabodha.description: Awakening or knowledge; often denotes spiritual realisation.

Yuktah.description: Steadfast or integrated; united in Yoga.

Brahmakara Vritti.description: A mental modification taking the form of Brahman; continuous contemplation of the Absolute.

Purushartha.description: Deliberate, conscious effort or action; also refers to the four aims of human life.

Brahma-bhootam.description: One who has become Brahman; Self-realised.

Shabda-brahman.description: The Vedic word or ritualistic portion of the Vedas.

Jnanis.description: Men of knowledge; scholars or philosophers.

Karmis.description: Men of action; those who perform works or rituals.

Antahkarana.description: The inner instrument; the mind-intellect complex.

Bhajana.description: Devotional worship or contemplation, especially of the Self.

Christ.description: Referenced as Lord Christ, he is used as a comparative figure to illustrate spiritual truths.

Rama.description: Mentioned as an example of a divine incarnation or sage who realized the Self.

Mohammed.description: Cited as one of the great prophets who realized and lived in the Self.

Mahavira.description: Referenced as a realized sage in the context of spiritual perfection.

India.description: The country of origin for the Bhagavad Gita and the philosophical schools discussed.

Jagat.description: A Sanskrit term meaning the world or the universe, especially as experienced through the senses, mind, and intellect.

Akasa.description: Sanskrit for 'ether' or 'space,' considered one of the five great elements in Indian philosophy.

Sad-Guru.description: A true spiritual teacher or enlightened master.

Devata.description: A deity or divine force invoked in worship or ritual.

Adhibhuta.description: Refers to the physical elements or the world of objects.

Adhidaiva.description: Pertains to the divine or the gods, often associated with the sense-organs.

Adhiyajna.description: Relates to sacrifice, particularly the principle presiding over all sacrifices or perceptions.

Upasaka.description: A devotee or worshipper, especially one engaged in spiritual practice.

Purusha.description: The spiritual principle or pure consciousness that enlivens matter.

Kama.description: Desire, especially for what is not present.

Raga.description: Attachment or affection for what one already possesses.

Balam.description: Strength or might, especially when devoid of desire and attachment.

Sadhaka.description: A spiritual aspirant or practitioner striving for realization.

A-dharma.description: Unrighteousness; actions or thoughts contrary to one's essential divine nature.

Eka bhaktih.description: Single-pointed devotion; unwavering focus on the Divine.

Upasya.description: The object of concentration or worship in spiritual practice.

Vikshepa.description: Mental agitation or distraction, caused by Rajas.

Avarana.description: Veiling or obscuration, caused by Tamas, which hides the Self.

punya.description: Merit; positive or virtuous actions that purify the mind.

papa.description: Sin; negative actions that create impurity and suffering.

ADHYATMA.description: The essential Self or the principle of Self-knowledge within an individual.

ADHIBHUTA.description: The perishable elements or the world of matter and phenomena.

ADHIDAIVA.description: The Indweller or presiding deity/faculty over the sense organs and mind.

ADHIYAJNA.description: The principle of sacrifice or the Self as the presiding factor in all acts of offering.

Puranas.description: Ancient Hindu texts containing mythological stories, traditions, and teachings.

Brahma-loka.description: The highest realm or world of Brahma, the Creator, attainable by souls through ritual and meditation.

Prashnopanishad.description: An Upanishadic text that discusses philosophical questions about creation and the nature of reality.

Pitrus.description: The ancestors; refers to the realm or world of the departed ancestors in Hindu belief.

YUGAS.description: Epochs or ages in Hindu cosmology, used to measure vast periods of time.

upasana.description: Upasana is devotional worship or meditative contemplation, especially on a chosen ideal or deity.

samsara.description: Samsara is the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth governed by karma.

OM.description: The sacred syllable symbolizing the Absolute, Brahman.

Krama Mukti.description: Gradual liberation; the doctrine that souls may attain liberation in stages.

Devayana.description: The 'Path of the gods'; the route taken by souls who attain gradual liberation.

Pitryana.description: The 'Path of the ancestors'; the route taken by souls who return to rebirth after enjoying heavenly realms.

Pralaya.description: Dissolution; the period when the manifest world returns to an unmanifest state.

Yoga-dharanam.description: Practice of concentration; the discipline of steadying the mind in meditation.

Adwaitins.description: Followers of Advaita Vedanta, the non-dualistic school of Indian philosophy.

Shrimad Bhagavata.description: A revered Purana that narrates the life and teachings of Krishna.

Omkara.description: The sacred syllable 'Om,' symbolizing the Absolute and the essence of the Vedas.

Turiya.description: The 'fourth' state of consciousness described in the Upanishads, beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

Soma.description: A ritual drink used in Vedic sacrifices, also personified as a deity.

Pitris.description: The ancestral spirits revered in Hindu rituals.

Bhutas.description: Elemental spirits or the five great elements in Indian cosmology.

Mundakopanishad.description: One of the principal Upanishads, known for its teachings on knowledge and liberation.

Samsarins.description: Beings caught in the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth (samsara).

Samsarin.description: An individual bound by samsara, the cycle of birth and death.

Samashti.description: The macrocosm, or the totality of creation.

Vyashti.description: The microcosm, or the individual being.

Ajya.description: Clarified butter (ghee) used as an offering in rituals.

Agni.description: Fire, both as an element and as the Vedic fire deity.

Hutam.description: Oblation or offering made into the sacred fire.

Om.description: The primordial sound and symbol of the Absolute.

Sama.description: The Sama Veda, or its chants.

Beejam Avyayam.description: The imperishable seed; the unchanging source of all.

Asat.description: Non-existence or the unreal; also, the effect.

Kirtana.description: Singing or chanting the glories of the Divine.

Dhridha-Vratah.description: One who is firm in vows or resolute.

Jnana Yajna.description: Jnana Yajna is the 'sacrifice of wisdom,' referring to the study, pursuit, and dissemination of spiritual knowledge.

Ishwara Darshana.description: Vision or realization of the Lord.

Atma Darshana.description: Vision or realization of the Self.

Sannyasa.description: Sannyasa is the path or state of renunciation, involving giving up worldly attachments, ego, and the fruits of actions.

Dharmatma.description: One whose nature is righteousness or who is established in dharma.

Striyah.description: Women; also used to indicate a feminine or emotional mind.

Varnashrama Dharma.description: The duties associated with one's class and stage of life.

Bhrigu.description: One of the Seven great Rishis, regarded as a chief sage in Hindu tradition.

Narada.description: A Deva-Rishi, renowned as a celestial sage and devotee, known for his wisdom and missionary zeal.

Kapila.description: A Muni and the founder of the Sankhya philosophy, recognized as a perfected thinker.

Prahlada.description: A Daitya prince celebrated for his unwavering devotion to Vishnu despite persecution by his father.

Ushana.description: A great seer and preceptor of the Daityas, sometimes identified as Shukra.

Kubera.description: The lord of wealth, associated with Yakshas and Rakshasas.

Yama.description: The mythical Lord of Death and controller of life and death.

Indra.description: The king of the gods and ruler of heaven, also referred to as Vasava.

Vishnu.description: One of the twelve Adityas, a principal deity representing preservation.

Chitraratha.description: A Gandharva, known as the chief among celestial musicians.

Vasuki.description: A serpent king, used as the churning rope in the myth of the milky ocean.

Varuna.description: Vedic deity governing the waters and oceans.

Vainateya.description: The king of birds and vehicle of Vishnu, also known as Vainateya.

Sama-Veda.description: One of the four Vedas, distinguished by its musical chants.

Rig-Veda.description: The oldest of the four Vedas, consisting mainly of hymns.

Chandogya Upanishad.description: A principal Upanishad, part of the Sama-Veda, known for its philosophical teachings.

Vrishnis.description: A clan or tribe descended from Vrishni, to which Krishna belonged.

Yadavas.description: A dynasty or clan to which Krishna belonged.

Kurus.description: The ruling dynasty of the Mahabharata era, including both Pandavas and Kauravas.

Jambu-dweepa.description: A term from ancient Hindu cosmology referring to the central continent of the world.

Himalayas.description: The great mountain range in northern India, revered as sacred.

Meru.description: A mythological mountain considered the center of the universe in Hindu cosmology.

Ashwattha.description: The Ashwattha is the sacred fig tree (Ficus Religiosa), used as an allegory for the Tree-of-life and symbolizing the universe or samsara.

Gayatri.description: A sacred Vedic metre and mantra, highly revered in Hindu tradition.

Airavata.description: The divine white elephant, mount of Indra.

Brihaspati.description: The spiritual teacher of the gods, associated with the planet Jupiter.

Marichi.description: Chief among the Maruts, wind deities.

Adityas.description: A group of solar deities, traditionally twelve in number.

Nakshatras.description: The lunar asterisms or constellations in Indian astronomy.

Vasus.description: Eight Vedic deities associated with natural phenomena.

Yakshas.description: Nature spirits associated with wealth and treasures.

Rakshasas.description: Mythical beings, often depicted as demons.

Danavas.description: A race of demons, sons of Danu, often opposing the Devas.

Daityas.description: A class of demons, descendants of Diti.

Vibhuti.description: Divine manifestations or glories of the Lord.

Jalpa.description: A type of argument aimed at defeating an opponent.

Vitanda.description: A type of argument focused on refuting the opponent without establishing one's own position.

Vaada.description: A logical, truth-seeking form of argument or debate.

Vishvato-mukhah.description: A term meaning 'facing all directions,' indicating omnipresence.

Hiranyagarbha.description: The 'cosmic womb' or golden egg, representing the source of creation.

Savitru.description: The Sun, especially as invoked in the Gayatri mantra.

Mahat.description: The cosmic intellect, the first principle of creation in Sankhya philosophy.

Ahamkara.description: The ego principle, the sense of individuality.

Sarva-loka-maheshwarah.description: Lord of all worlds; the Supreme Self ruling over all fields of experience.

Loka.description: A world or realm of experience.

Purushottama.description: The Supreme Purusha, or highest Self.

Bhaava samanvitah.description: Endowed with loving consciousness or attitude.

Mat-chittah.description: One whose mind is wholly absorbed in the Lord.

Savikalpa.description: A state of samadhi where some duality or distinction remains.

Nirvikalpa.description: A state of samadhi where all distinctions and dualities are transcended.

Jijnasa.description: The desire to know or inquire.

Satsanga.description: Association with the wise or with spiritual company.

Japa.description: Repetition of a mantra as a spiritual practice.

Sadhya.description: The goal or that which is to be achieved.

Jayadratha.description: A warrior chief allied with the Kauravas, mentioned among those already doomed.

Brahma.description: Brahma is the Creator god in Hinduism, depicted as the Lord of Creation and source of all action and creation.

Shiva.description: The Annihilator and part of the divine trinity, also called Isham, seen in the Cosmic Form.

Ashwins.description: The twin horsemen, divine beings associated with healing and service, seen in the Universal Form.

Kaurava.description: The dynasty of Dhritarashtra's sons, opposed to the Pandavas.

Badrinath.description: A sacred Himalayan location associated with Vyasa and spiritual practice.

Vishwaroopa.description: The Universal Form of the Lord, as revealed to Arjuna in this chapter.

Yadava.description: A term referring to Krishna's clan or lineage.

Rishi.description: A sage or seer, often referenced as witnessing or praising the Universal Form.

Siddha.description: A perfected being, spiritually advanced and present in the cosmic vision.

Gandharva.description: Celestial musicians in Hindu mythology, present in the Universal Form.

Yaksha.description: Nature spirits or guardians of wealth, included among the beings witnessing the vision.

Asura.description: Asuras are a class of powerful beings or demons opposed to the gods, representing demonic or devilish qualities contrary to divine virtues.

Vishwe-devas.description: A group of universal deities in Vedic tradition.

Ushmapa.description: A class of ancestral spirits or beings associated with ritual offerings.

Marut.description: Storm deities, part of the divine hosts seen in the Universal Form.

Aditya.description: Solar deities, sons of Aditi, referenced as part of the cosmic vision.

Vasu.description: Elemental deities representing natural forces, included in the Universal Form.

Bhakti.description: Devotion; loving worship or surrender to the Divine.

Vishwa.description: The totality of experience; the universe as perceived through body, mind, and intellect.

Kaala-chakra.description: The wheel of time; the cyclical nature of creation and destruction.

Mahavakya.description: A 'great saying' from the Upanishads, expressing the identity of the individual Self with the Absolute.

avyakta.description: Avyakta is the unmanifested; that which is not yet manifest as name and form.

indriya-agocaram.description: That which is beyond the range of the sense organs.

vyakta.description: Vyakta is the manifest; that which is perceptible to the senses.

Akshara.description: The imperishable; that which does not perish or decay.

Anirdeshyam.description: The indefinable; that which cannot be defined or described.

Achintyam.description: Unthinkable or inconceivable; beyond the capacity of thought.

Achalam.description: Immovable; that which does not move or change position.

Dhruvam.description: Eternal; that which is constant and unchanging over time.

Dhyana.description: Meditation; focused contemplation on a spiritual object or truth.

Abhyasa-Yoga.description: The Yoga of constant practice; repeated effort to steady the mind.

Aarambha.description: Beginning; the start of an undertaking or action.

Anapekshah.description: Free from dependence; not relying on external objects or circumstances.

Shuchih.description: Pure; clean in body, mind, and surroundings.

Dakshah.description: Alert; efficient and skillful in action.

Udaseenah.description: Unconcerned; maintaining indifference to minor disturbances.

Mouna.description: Silence; both external and internal quietude.

Acharyas.description: Respected teachers or preceptors in Indian philosophical traditions.

Hindu Scriptures.description: Sacred texts of Hinduism, including the Vedas, Upanishads, and the Bhagavad Geeta.

RISHIS.description: Ancient sages or seers who composed the hymns and philosophical texts of Hinduism.

Moola-Prakriti.description: The primordial, unmanifested matter or root nature in Sankhya philosophy.

Yogarudha.description: A state of yogic integration or realization.

Purusha Sooktam.description: A hymn from the Rig Veda describing the cosmic being, Purusha.

Rig Veda.description: One of the oldest Hindu scriptures, containing hymns and philosophical teachings.

Sankhya Yoga.description: The path of knowledge and discrimination as taught in the Sankhya philosophy.

PARAMATMAN.description: The Supreme Self or Universal Spirit in Vedanta.

Parameshwara.description: The Supreme Lord, the ultimate reality underlying all existence.

Kshetra.description: The Field; refers to the body or the realm of matter.

Kshetrajna.description: The Knower-of-the-Field; the conscious principle that knows the Field.

Tattwas.description: Principles or elements; fundamental categories in Sankhya philosophy.

Samghata.description: Aggregate; the assemblage of body and its components.

Vairagya.description: Dispassion or detachment from sense objects.

Jnana-gamyam.description: That which is to be reached by knowledge.

Jneyam.description: That which is to be known.

Bhoktri.description: The enjoyer; the one who experiences pleasure and pain.

Sattwic.description: Of the quality of sattva; pure, harmonious, and balanced.

Kutasthah.description: The changeless substratum; the unchanging Self.

Shri Shankaracharya.description: A renowned Advaita Vedanta philosopher and commentator on the Bhagavad Gita.

Brahmaloka.description: The highest realm of existence, associated with Brahma and supreme joy, as per Hindu cosmology.

Agamas.description: Scriptural texts in Hinduism that provide instructions on rituals, temple construction, and philosophy.

Kuru.description: A reference to the Kuru dynasty, to which Arjuna belongs.

Jivatman.description: The individual soul or embodied self, distinct from the Supreme Self.

Anatman.description: That which is not the Self; the non-self or material aspect.

jiva.description: Jiva is the individual soul or embodied self, subject to birth and death.

nir-upadhika.description: Without attributes or conditioning; the unconditioned Absolute.

sa-upadhika.description: With attributes or conditioning; the conditioned aspect of Brahman.

muni.description: A sage or contemplative, one who reflects deeply.

Anandagiri.description: A commentator referenced for his explanation of the symbolism of the Ashwattha tree.

Kathopanishad.description: An Upanishad referenced for its allegorical use of the Peepal-tree.

PURUSHA.description: A term for the cosmic spirit or Self; used here for both the perishable and imperishable principles.

KOOTASTHAH.description: The immutable, imperishable Self that remains unchanged amidst change.

PURUSHOTTAMA.description: The Supreme Spirit, the highest Self, transcending both the perishable and imperishable.

Veda.description: The Vedas are the ancient sacred scriptures of Hinduism, regarded as the source of spiritual knowledge.

Samskaras.description: Mental impressions or conditioning formed by past actions.

Antah-karana.description: The inner instrument; the mind-intellect equipment.

Vaishvaanara.description: The digestive fire; the aspect of the Divine that digests food in living beings.

Apana.description: The vital force responsible for excretion and downward movement in the body.

Kshara.description: The perishable aspect of reality; that which is subject to change.

Brahma-vidya.description: The science or knowledge of Brahman, the ultimate reality.

Bhakti-Yoga.description: The path of devotion as a means to spiritual realization.

Vedic.description: Pertaining to the Vedas, the ancient sacred texts of Hinduism.

Charvakas.description: A school of ancient Indian materialist and atheist philosophy, emphasizing direct perception and denial of afterlife.

Abhayam.description: Fearlessness; the absence of fear, considered a divine quality.

Daana.description: Charity or alms-giving; the act of giving to others selflessly.

dama.description: Control of the senses; self-restraint in relation to sensory pleasures.

Swaadhyaaya.description: Study of the scriptures; self-study or recitation of sacred texts.

Arjavam.description: Uprightness; honesty and straightforwardness in thought, word, and deed.

Ahimsa.description: Non-violence; harmlessness towards all beings in thought, word, and action.

Satyam.description: Truth; adherence to truthfulness and honesty.

Akrodha.description: Absence of anger; maintaining an even temper and self-control.

Tyaga.description: Renunciation; the spirit of letting go of attachments and desires.

Apaishunam.description: Absence of malice; refraining from slander or malicious speech.

Aloluptvam.description: Non-covetousness; freedom from greed and desire for others' possessions.

Achaapalam.description: Absence of fickleness; steadiness and restraint in physical movements.

Tejas.description: Vigour; spiritual brilliance or inner radiance.

Kshamaa.description: Forgiveness; patience and the ability to forgive others.

Dhriti.description: Fortitude; perseverance and steadfastness in the face of challenges.

Shoucham.description: Purity; cleanliness of body, mind, and environment.

Adroha.description: Absence of hatred; non-injury and goodwill towards all.

Na-ati-maanitaa.description: Absence of over-pride; humility and lack of excessive self-importance.

Dambha.description: Hypocrisy or ostentation; pretension of virtue without sincerity.

Parushya.description: Harshness; roughness or cruelty in speech or action.

ajnanam.description: Ignorance; lack of spiritual knowledge or awareness.

Daivic.description: Divine; pertaining to godly or virtuous qualities.

Rakshasic.description: Incorrigibly indifferent; a type of being characterized by ignorance and inertia.

Achara.description: Right conduct; proper behavior in accordance with dharma.

Asatyam.description: Untruth; falsehood or lack of adherence to truth.

An-Ishwaram.description: Without a Lord; denial of a supreme governing principle or God.

Shreyas.description: The highest good; that which leads to ultimate well-being and liberation.

Prakarana.description: Subsidiary texts; explanatory treatises that clarify scriptural teachings.

Nishtha.description: Steadfastness or firm resolve, especially in spiritual practice.

Pretas.description: Ghosts or spirits of the dead, invoked by tamasic individuals.

Tapaswin.description: One who practices austerity or self-discipline.

Dakshina.description: A gift or offering, often given to priests or teachers as part of a ritual.

Dwija.description: Literally 'twice-born,' referring to those who have undergone a spiritual initiation, especially Brahmins.

Shaareeram Tapas.description: Austerity of the body, involving physical purity and discipline.

Yaama.description: A unit of time, traditionally three hours; used in the context of food freshness.

Amedhyam.description: Impure or unclean, especially in the context of food.

Nishiddha.description: Forbidden actions, prohibited by the scriptures.

Naimittika.description: Occasional duties, performed on special occasions.

Anuroopa.description: According to or in conformity with (one's nature).

Tat.description: That; used to indicate the universal truth or the ultimate reality.

Om Tat Sat.description: A triple designation of Brahman, symbolizing the Absolute, the Universal Truth, and Existence.

Kumbhakarna.description: A character from Lanka, symbolic of a Tamasic 'doer,' known for sleeping six months and eating the rest.

Kapila's Saankhya Yoga.description: The system of yoga and philosophy attributed to sage Kapila, focusing on the three gunas.

Lanka.description: The kingdom ruled by Ravana in the Ramayana, referenced here for its characters.

Ashta-vasu.description: The eight Vasus, elemental deities presiding over Time.

Ishaavasya Upanishad.description: A principal Upanishad emphasizing the pervasiveness of the Divine.

Tyaaga.description: Another spelling of Tyaga, denoting abandonment.

Rajasic.description: Passionate; relating to the guna of activity, desire, and restlessness.

Tamasic.description: Dull; relating to the guna of inertia, ignorance, and darkness.

Karma Phala.description: The fruits or results of actions.

Adhishthaanam.description: Seat; the body as the basis of action.

Triputi.description: The triad of knower, known, and knowledge.

Niyatam.description: Obligatory or prescribed (as in obligatory action).

Bandham.description: Bondage; the state of being bound by ignorance or attachment.

Pravritti.description: Action or engagement in worldly pursuits.

Nivritti.description: Withdrawal or renunciation from worldly pursuits.

Jnaanam.description: Knowledge; especially spiritual or higher knowledge.

Parijnaataa.description: The knower; the subject or experiencer.

Nidraa.description: Sleep; also used philosophically as non-apprehension of Reality.

Brahma-Bhootah.description: One who has realized or become identified with Brahman.

Naishkarmya.description: Actionlessness; the state of being free from the sense of doership.

Naishkarmya-Siddhi.description: The state of perfection in actionlessness.

Anasooyah.description: One who is free from malice.

Prasannaatmaa.description: One with a tranquil or serene mind.
